chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Numerical Methods? Foundations of Option Pricing Beyond Closed-Form

lessons.title: Risk-Neutral Valuation: The Idea Every Numerical Method Relies On

children.text: Every numerical method this course builds, a binomial tree in Chapters 2 and 3, a finite difference grid in Chapter 4, is a different way of computing the same underlying idea. Before touching either, it is worth seeing that idea in its simplest possible form, one period, two outcomes, because everything after this lesson is just this argument repeated many times over.
The Puzzle: Two Ways to Discount a Future Payoff

The obvious way to value any future payoff is to estimate its expected value under the real-world odds of each outcome, then discount that expectation back at a rate that reflects the risk involved. That is exactly how a DCF values a stock. It runs into trouble immediately for an option: what discount rate compensates for an option's risk? An option's risk changes constantly as the stock moves, so there is no single, stable number to use, and estimating the market's true odds of the stock ending up or down is itself a forecasting exercise nobody can pin down precisely. Black-Scholes, and every numerical method in this course, sidesteps the whole problem with a different approach.
A Two-State World: The Simplest Possible Market

markDefs.definition: The principle that identical future payoffs must cost the same today, otherwise a risk-free profit could be locked in by buying the cheap version and selling the expensive one. Every pricing argument in this course rests on it.

children.text: Take a stock trading today at ₹100. Over the next year it will move to exactly one of two prices, ₹120 or ₹90, nothing in between. The risk-free rate for the year is 5%. A call option struck at ₹100 pays ₹20 if the stock ends at ₹120, and ₹0 if it ends at ₹90. The question is what that call is worth today, and the answer comes from

Build a portfolio out of the stock and a risk-free loan that produces exactly ₹20 in the up state and exactly ₹0 in the down state, the same payoff as the call, no matter what happens. If such a portfolio exists, its cost today must equal the call's price today, since two things with identical payoffs in every future state must trade at the same price. Buy delta shares of stock and put B rupees into (or borrow B rupees from) the risk-free asset.

body.caption: The number of shares that makes the portfolio's up-state and down-state payoffs move exactly like the call's.

children.text: Solving Delta times 120 plus B times 1.05 equals 20 gives B = -57.14, a borrowing of ₹57.14 today at the risk-free rate. Check it against the down state: 0.667 times 90 minus 57.14 times 1.05 works out to ₹0, matching the call's down-state payoff exactly. The replicating portfolio is confirmed.

body.label: Cost of the replicating portfolio today
body.context: By no-arbitrage, this must also be the call's fair price today

body.text: Look back over that entire calculation. Nowhere did it use the actual, real-world probability of the stock going up to ₹120 versus down to ₹90. Not once. The price came out of Su, Sd, S0, K, and r alone. That is the whole trick, and it is not a simplification, it is exact.

children.text: There is a second, equivalent way to reach the same ₹9.52 that makes the name obvious. Find the probability p of the up-move that would make the stock itself, on average, earn exactly the risk-free rate, nothing more, nothing less, as if investors did not demand any extra return for holding a risky asset.

body.caption: The risk-neutral probability of the up-move. Chapter 2 formalizes this for a full multi-step tree using the Cox-Ross-Rubinstein parameterization; for now, the arithmetic above is all you need.

children.text: Discount the call's expected payoff under this p at the risk-free rate: (0.5 times 20 plus 0.5 times 0) divided by 1.05 equals ₹9.52, the identical answer as the replicating portfolio. This p is not the market's actual belief about the stock, and it is almost never equal to it. It is a mathematical construct, the probability that would apply if every investor were indifferent to risk. Formally, in mathematical finance this is called the equivalent martingale measure, but risk-neutral probability is the working name you will use throughout this course.

columns.label: Real-World (Physical) Probability
points: Reflects actual investor beliefs about the odds of an up or down move
Needed to forecast a stock's own expected return, growth projections, or a fund's expected NAV
Requires estimating a risk premium, subjective and never precisely observable
Different investors can reasonably disagree on this number

columns.label: Risk-Neutral Probability
points: A constructed number that makes every asset earn exactly the risk-free rate in expectation
Needed to price a derivative on the stock, not to forecast the stock itself
Backed out entirely from no-arbitrage, no risk premium estimate required
Every arbitrage-free market participant must agree on this number, or a risk-free profit exists

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: In the two-state example above, suppose the market's real-world probability of the stock rising to ₹120 is actually 80%, not 50%. What happens to the call's price of ₹9.52?
options: It rises, since the payoff is now more likely
It stays exactly ₹9.52, unaffected by the real-world probability
It needs to be recalculated using 80% as the discounting probability
body.explanation: The no-arbitrage replicating-portfolio argument pins the price down using only S0, Su, Sd, K, and r. Real-world probability never enters the calculation. Any investor, however bullish or bearish about the stock's real chances, must agree on ₹9.52 or a risk-free arbitrage opens up between the option and the replicating portfolio.

body.title: Explaining It to a Retail Investor
body.scenario: A retail investor tells you they are convinced Reliance Industries has a 70% chance of closing above ₹3,000 on the NSE by a given expiry, and asks why the options market does not simply price the call option using that 70% probability.
body.prompt: How would you explain, in plain terms, why option prices don't work that way, and what the investor should actually do with a strong 70% conviction?
body.modelAnswer: Option prices come from the cost of replicating the option's payoff using the underlying stock and a risk-free loan or deposit, not from any one trader's forecast, so a single person's 70% belief has no direct channel into the market price. If it did, and the market simply adopted whoever's forecast was loudest, there would be no way to profit from being right more often than the market. The correct move for someone with a genuine, well-reasoned 70% conviction is not to expect the option's price to already reflect it, but to buy the call and profit if that view turns out correct, exactly the trade that only makes sense because the market price is not already using their number.

body.code:
# Two-state replicating portfolio and risk-neutral check
S0, Su, Sd, K, r = 100, 120, 90, 100, 0.05
Cu, Cd = max(Su - K, 0), max(Sd - K, 0)

delta = (Cu - Cd) / (Su - Sd)
B = (Cu - delta * Su) / (1 + r)
replicating_cost = delta * S0 + B

p = ((1 + r) * S0 - Sd) / (Su - Sd)
risk_neutral_price = (p * Cu + (1 - p) * Cd) / (1 + r)

print(f"Replicating portfolio cost: Rs {replicating_cost:.2f}")
print(f"Risk-neutral probability p: {p:.2f}")
print(f"Risk-neutral discounted price: Rs {risk_neutral_price:.2f}")
body.caption: Both routes, building the replicating portfolio and discounting under the risk-neutral probability, land on the same Rs 9.52, exactly as they must under no-arbitrage.

children.text: Why Every Method in This Course Leans on This

A binomial tree is this exact two-state calculation, done at every node, working backward from expiry to today, over as many steps as needed. A finite difference method solves the Black-Scholes partial differential equation directly, and that PDE is itself derived from the same replicating-portfolio, no-arbitrage argument, which is why its drift term uses the risk-free rate r rather than the stock's real-world expected return. Different mechanics, same economic idea underneath both.

body.text: Price a derivative by replicating its payoff with the underlying and a risk-free loan, not by forecasting the future. Every method in this course computes that replication, one recursively through a tree, the other by solving the equation it satisfies directly.

points: A derivative's price is pinned down by the cost of a portfolio that replicates its payoff exactly, using the underlying stock and a risk-free loan.
Real-world probabilities of the stock going up or down never enter that calculation, only the up and down price levels, the strike, and the risk-free rate do.
Risk-neutral probability is the probability that would make the stock itself earn exactly the risk-free rate on average. It is a pricing device, not anyone's actual market view.
In the ₹100 stock example, going to ₹120 or ₹90, at a 5% risk-free rate, a ₹100-strike call is worth ₹9.52, whether the real-world odds of the up-move are 10% or 90%.

Binomial trees apply this same replication recursively across many steps. Finite difference methods encode it directly in the Black-Scholes PDE. Both rest on the identical foundation built in this lesson.
